title: Sure Thing Principle
body_html:
Sure Thing Principle

The sure-thing principle says that a common consequence in a lottery mixture does not affect strict preference between the non-common parts.

If independence holds, then for any lotteries $L_1,L_2,L_3,L_4$ and $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $$ \operatorname{StrictPref}([\alpha L_1,(1-\alpha)L_3], [\alpha L_2,(1-\alpha)L_3]) $$ if and only if $$ \operatorname{StrictPref}([\alpha L_1,(1-\alpha)L_4], [\alpha L_2,(1-\alpha)L_4]). $$
proof_html:
Sketch

When $\alpha=0$, both sides compare a lottery with itself and strict preference is impossible. When $\alpha>0$, apply independence once to remove $L_3$ and once to insert $L_4$.

References

  • [MSZ, Chapter 2, Exercise 2.12] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, Game Theory, references/GameTheory.pdf. The sure-thing principle follows from independence.
